McDonald's is an American fast food chain, founded in 1940 as a single restaurant run by the brothers Richard and Maurice McDonald in San Bernardino, California. It grew into one of the largest restaurant companies in the world, with more than 40,000 outlets in over 100 countries.

In 1948 the brothers cut their menu to a few items, mainly burgers, fries and milkshakes, and reorganised the kitchen like a factory line. Each worker did one simple task, and food was ready in moments. They called it the Speedee Service System. It applied to food the ideas Henry Ford had used to build cars.

The salesman Ray Kroc saw its potential. He became their franchise agent in 1955, opened his own restaurant near Chicago, and in 1961 bought the brothers out. His model was franchising: local owners ran the restaurants, but every one followed the same rules, so a burger tasted the same everywhere. The growth of car ownership and suburbs in post-war America suited it well.

From the 1970s McDonald's went global, reaching Japan in 1971, Moscow in 1990 and China the same year. It adapted menus, selling no beef in India, for example. Its golden arches became a symbol of American influence and of globalisation, praised for efficiency and criticised for its effect on diets, farming, wages and local food cultures. Like jazz or Hollywood, it shows how American ways of living spread across the world in the 20th century.
